The robustness claims overstate the consistency of the results. CelebA worst-group accuracy improves only from 9.6% to 10.4% in Table 3 and from 72.8% to 73.1% in Table 5. CivilComments prompting improves worst-group accuracy but reduces average accuracy from 80.2% to 71.0%. Tables 5–6 provide no uncertainty estimates supporting claims of significant superiority.

The defining no-counterexample experiment is insufficiently specified: validation is used for model selection, but whether minority groups are also removed from validation is unclear. Group definitions and retained sample counts, particularly for CivilComments, need clarification. Reproducibility is further limited by missing filtering prompts, the smoothing-window setting, the number of repeated runs, and the promised code URL.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: discovering model shortcuts that available validation counterexamples may fail to expose. Producing interpretable concept names makes the approach potentially useful for model auditing.

Table 3 provides meaningful positive evidence: WASP regularization improves worst-group accuracy over ERM from 43.2% to 57.9% on Waterbirds and from 18.6% to 31.3% on CivilComments. Comparisons with random concepts and LG strengthen these results.

The ImageNet experiments quantify selected failure cases using 1,000 images per prompt, report induced-class predictions as well as accuracy, and demonstrate accuracy degradation across many classifier architectures.
Evaluation spans image and text tasks and explores both regularization and prompt augmentation. The method is relatively simple, and the appendix supplies extensive concept lists and model results.
weaknesses: The novelty of the weight-space formulation is insufficiently established. For the linear classifier studied here, multiplying weights by concept embeddings is simply evaluating concept logits, closely related to the language-probing approach described for DrML. DrML is not compared experimentally, and there is no comparison with untrained class-name weights or explicit weight differences to establish what was newly learned during fine-tuning.

The central interpretation of the scores as learned spuriousness remains inadequately validated. Equation 2 measures separation from the least-aligned class; a large value does not necessarily imply class specificity or increased class probability when the concept appears. Semantic filtering also does not establish causal irrelevance: the supposedly class-neutral lists include avocado for guacamole and hate/troll for offensive comments. These examples require contextual validation, and no systematic detection precision or independent annotation study is provided.

ImageNet validation covers only three selected concept–class scenarios, without reporting the success rate across the discovered concepts. Separately generated prompts also change scene composition and object prominence: the newspaper example introduces a person and chair and places the dog in the person's lap. Matched image edits and comparable low-scoring distractors are needed to isolate the proposed concept's effect. High accuracy on object-only synthetic images does not establish that the composite images are in distribution.

The counterexample-free experiment is underspecified. Section 4 uses validation accuracy for early stopping, but Section 5.2 does not clearly establish whether counterexamples are also removed from validation/model selection. The exact group-removal procedure and retained sample counts, particularly for overlapping CivilComments identities, are missing. Table 3 also omits the frozen zero-shot foundation model, an important baseline when fine-tuning on perfectly confounded data.

Claims of consistently superior robustness overstate the results. In Table 5, CelebA worst-group accuracy improves only from 72.8% to 73.1%, while average accuracy falls from 87.7% to 85.7%. CivilComments gains worst-group accuracy but loses 9.2 points of average accuracy, and no competing discovery method is evaluated there. Tables 5–6 lack uncertainty estimates; the CivilComments comparison also changes the prompt template from bare class labels to sentences.

The ablations do not isolate the contribution of weight-based ranking from candidate extraction, semantic filtering, initialization, or prompt selection. The approach still depends on a finite vocabulary extracted from training captions/text, limiting claims that it bypasses exhaustive candidate coverage. Applicability is demonstrated for linear heads over frozen aligned representations, rather than general fine-tuned network weights.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the stated code link is absent, and filtering prompts, smoothing-window settings, and repeated-run details are not supplied. Algorithm 1 also appears inconsistent with the main description: lines 14–15 compare concept scores against a rank-valued cutoff rather than selecting the top-ranked concepts. These gaps impede verification of the central results.
